history_of_present_illness: Dysentery is a symptom-complex characterized by small, frequently passed mucous or muco-sanguinolent stools and painful intestinal gripings (tormina) or spasmodic contractions of the sphincter ani (tenesmus). The stool typically consists of greenish-yellow or dirty brown mucus intimately mixed with altered blood, or a whitish to grayish muco-purulent mass with blood streaks or flecks, often suspended in small amounts of serous, sanguineous, or feculent discharges. Tormina are griping colicky pains centering about the umbilicus or along the large intestine, while tenesmus refers to painful straining due to the sensation of incomplete defecation. The closer the dysenteric process is to the rectum, the greater the tenesmus; closer to the caecum, the greater the tormina. In flagellate dysenteries, young children may experience insidious onset with fever and stools containing much mucus with little blood. Lamblia infections can cause diarrheal attacks, sometimes with yellow ochre stools and common relapses. Balantidium coli infection typically begins insidiously with diarrhea followed by dysentery and may lead to severe anemia. Dysenteric manifestations can also occur in terminal kala-azar, algid pernicious malaria, coccidial infections, and various helminthic infections (trematodes, cestodes, nematodes), where stools may show mucus with clotted blood and diagnostic ova. Bacterial dysenteries vary, with Morgan's bacillus causing summer diarrhea in children, and 'ekiri' being a fatal dysentery-like disease in Japanese children. Spirillar dysentery presents without fever. Mechanical irritants or poisons like arsenic, antimony, and mercury can also induce dysenteric symptoms, often accompanied by marked abdominal pain.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Dysentery, described by Hippocrates and believed to exist in Egypt and India for centuries, is predominantly caused by bacillary or amoebic infections. Our understanding of these conditions significantly advanced after Shiga's reporting of his bacillus in 1898. Flagellate dysenteries, particularly lambliasis, are common in mice and rats, suggesting these rodents may spread infection via their feces contaminating human food. Balantidium coli dysentery is usually found in individuals caring for hogs, as the ciliate is a hog commensal, with infections reported globally. Isospora hominis infections have been reported chiefly among soldiers in Gallipoli. Oesophagostomum species have caused dysentery in African natives and Brazilians. Morgan's bacillus, a cause of bacillary dysentery, is often found in flies from affected households. 'Ekiri' is a dysentery-like epidemic disease occurring in young children in Japan. Pseudomonas pyocyaneus infections causing dysentery are noted in debilitated children in the tropics. Mechanical irritants like bristles mixed with food have caused poisoning with dysenteric manifestations in North China.
vitals: Fever may be present in the insidious onset of flagellate dysenteries in children. Spirillar dysentery is characterized by an absence of fever.
physical_exam: Physical findings include painful spasmodic contractions of the sphincter ani (tenesmus), often leading to straining, and griping colicky pains (tormina) centered about the umbilicus or along the large intestine. A severe form of anemia may be noted in cases of ciliate dysentery caused by Balantidium coli.
labs_and_diagnostics: The characteristic stool in dysentery is mucous or muco-sanguinolent, often small, greenish-yellow, dirty brown, or whitish-gray, with altered blood intimately admixed or streaked. Mucoid masses may be suspended in serous, sanguineous, or feculent discharges. Diagnostic findings for specific causes include: Encysted Lamblia (oval, 10x7µ, with a curved central line and two lateral chromatin dots, abundant in feces); vegetative Lamblia (15µ long, 4 pairs of flagella, tumbling motion). Balantidium coli is a large, actively motile, oval ciliate (60-100µ long by 50-70µ broad), easily detected microscopically; encysted forms are round. In helminthic dysenteries, diagnostic ova may be found in the mucus-coated stool, and a high eosinophilia is present in Schistosoma infections. Isospora hominis oocysts are ovoid (28x14 microns), narrowed at one end, containing two sporocysts each with four sporozoites, unsegmented when first passed. Bacterial identification includes: Morgan's bacillus (motile, indol positive, slight gas in glucose bouillon, no change in mannite, no primary acidity in litmus milk); 'ekiri' organism (very motile, produces gas and acid in glucose but not lactose, sometimes indol production, a member of the Gärtner group); Spirillar forms (Gram negative, noncultivable). The color of stools may be suggestive in Pyocyaneus infections. Figure 58 illustrates important pathogenic intestinal protozoa including E. coli, E. histolytica, Eimeria stiedae, Isospora bigemina, Trichomonas intestinalis, Lamblia intestinalis, and Balantidium coli, detailing their morphological features for identification.
differential_diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include bacillary dysentery (Shiga, Flexner group, B. Morgan No. 1, 'ekiri' organism, Spirillar forms, B. pyocyaneus, streptococci, atypical B. coli, Gärtner group), amoebic dysentery (Entamoeba histolytica), flagellate dysenteries (Lamblia intestinalis, Trichomonas intestinalis, Chilomastix mesnili), ciliate dysenteries (Balantidium coli), terminal kala-azar (Leishmania donovani), algid pernicious malaria (Plasmodium falciparum), coccidial infection (Isospora hominis), helminthic dysenteries (Schistosoma mansoni, S. japonicum, Gastrodiscus hominis, Heterophyes heterophyes, Oesophagostomum brumpti/stephanostomum), intestinal myiasis, paratyphoid infections (presenting as colitis, entero-colitis, or gastro-enteritis), ptomaine poisoning (Gärtner group), mechanical irritants (bristles), poisonous substances (arsenic, antimony, mercury), cancer of the rectum, syphilis of the rectum, intussusception (with bloody rather than muco-sanguineous stools), terminal stages of chronic diseases (tuberculosis, cardiac affections), and chronic nephritis leading to uremia (catarrhal or diphtheritic colitis).
management_and_clinical_course: For flagellate dysenteries, calomel alone or with ipecac has shown good results. Enemata of organic silver salts and bismuth salicylate have been recommended. However, lambliasis often recurs, and treatments with bismuth, salol, thymol, cyllin, methylene blue, turpentine, or beta-naphthol have not always been encouraging. Administering drugs via a duodenal tube, such as ipecac for amoebic dysentery, and sulfur for lambliasis, has been suggested. For ciliate dysenteries caused by Balantidium coli, ipecac, emetine, arsenic, and quinine are generally of little value. Organic silver compounds like protargol, as well as methylene blue enemata (1:3000) and 2-grain pills by mouth, have been recommended. The 'ekiri' type of dysentery in Japan is noted to be a very fatal disease.

images.caption: Fig. 58.—Important pathogenic Protozoa of the intestinal tract. (1a) Motile E. coli. Note large amount of peripheral arrangement of chromatin in nucleus. (1b) Encysted E. coli. Note larger size than E. histolytica cyst, 8 ring form nuclei and absence of chromidial bodies. (2) Motile E. histolytica from acute dysenteric stool. Note histolytica nucleus with scanty chromatin. (3) Tetragena type of E. histolytica from case of chronic dysentery. Note greater amount of chromatin and central karyosome with centriole. (4a) Preëncysted E. histolytica from carrier. Note small size and heavy peripheral ring of chromatin in nucleus making this feature of chromatin in nucleus similar to the larger E. coli. (4b) Encysted E. histolytica from dysentery convalescent. Note small size, 4 ring nuclei and a dark chromatin staining mass, “chromidial body.” (5a and 5b) Motile and encysted cultural amoebae from Manila water supply. (6a and 6b) Oocyst and sporozoite production in 4 spores of Eimeria stiedae. (7a and 7b) Oocyst with 2 sporoblasts and oocyst with 2 spores containing 4 sporozoites of Isospora bigemina. (8a and 8b) Vegetative and encysted Trichomonas intestinalis. (9a and 9b) Vegetative and encysted Lamblia intestinalis. (10) Balantidium coli. Illustrations of amoebae from Walker—others from Doflein.
